summary: Added more partly timbered land in California to the Stony Creek National Forest and redrew its boundaries.
Rewrote a section of the 1906 consular service order so consular clerks, vice consuls, interpreters and similar officers appointed by examination could be promoted on ability and efficiency.
Let Charles L. Murphy be permanently appointed a skilled laborer at the Bureau of Fisheries' central station, since no other eligibles had his qualifications.
Redrew the Lincoln National Forest in New Mexico Territory, adding some partly timbered lands and cutting others out.
Created the Sacramento National Forest from partly timbered public lands in New Mexico Territory, including part of the area once in the Lincoln National Forest.
Enlarged the Beaver National Forest in Utah with additional lands partly covered with timber.
Expanded Utah's Manti National Forest to take in more partly timbered land.
Excused federal workers in Washington who belonged to Civil War veterans' societies from duty on May 2, 1907, so they could attend the unveiling of the Gen. George B. McClellan statue.
Allowed Frederick L. Dunlap of Michigan to be appointed associate chemist and member of the food and drug inspection in the Department of Agriculture without examination.
Named Huntington Wilson acting Secretary of State.
Added partly timbered lands in Utah to the Fish Lake National Forest.
Let Civil War veteran Harrison L. Deam, a temporary watchman at the Interior Department, be appointed permanently without regard to civil-service rules.
Allowed three Agriculture Department student assistants to be appointed after noncompetitive exams: James D. Rowan Jr. and Charles L. Gooch as gardeners, and William Grant as a laboratory helper.
Allowed Elsie E. Lower of Pennsylvania, an Agriculture Department student assistant, to be appointed clerk and artist without examination.
Let Nathaniel C. Murray, a special field agent in the Agriculture Department's Bureau of Statistics, be appointed assistant statistician without meeting civil-service rules.
Postponed the abolition of the Florida surveyor general's office to June 30, 1908.
Reserved lands in Alaska for educational purposes until the General Land Office could survey them.
Created Cinder Cone National Monument in California, protecting the Cinder Cone, its lava field, Snag Lake and Lake Bidwell as examples of volcanic activity of great scientific interest.
Set aside Lassen Peak in California as a national monument, citing its place at the southern end of the Cascade Range's line of extinct volcanoes.
Allowed Claude I. Parker of Louisiana to be appointed law librarian or to a clerical post in the General Land Office without regard to civil-service rules.
Returned to the public domain lands in Washington that had been allotted to the Indians Snain-Chucks and Paul.
Let James Powers be employed by the Census Bureau on experimental work developing tabulating machinery, without a civil-service examination.

Set the pay of Immigration Commission members Jeremiah W. Jenks and William R. Wheeler at $7,500 a year, and Charles P. Neill's at $7,500 including his pay as Commissioner of Labor, dating from April 1, 1907.
Brought the 33 laborers in the Boston collector's office into the classified civil service, and let department heads do the same wherever laborers split time between classified and unclassified work.
Changed a civil-service exception so all navigating positions on the Army Quartermaster's torpedo and mine planters, not just firemen, were excepted from examination.
Transferred the vessel Zafiro from the Navy Department to the War Department.

Directed that from June 1, 1907, official communications to and from executive officers of Arizona, Hawaii, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Porto Rico, Alaska, Indian Territory, Samoa and Guam go through the Secretary of the Interior.

Authorized the Interstate Commerce Commission to appoint up to fifteen special agents or examiners before July 1, 1907, who could join the classified service after six months' probation and a noncompetitive exam.
Let John D. Torrey, a temporary topographic draftsman in the Coast and Geodetic Survey with twenty years of Navy Department service, be appointed permanently without regard to civil-service rules.
Redrew the boundaries of the Nome and Fairbanks land districts in Alaska and created a new Juneau land district.
Canceled the planned transfer of Fort St. Michael Military Reservation lands in Alaska to the Interior Department, keeping them reserved for military purposes.
Opened Huntley Project farm units on ceded Crow Reservation land in Montana to settlement under the Reclamation Act from July 22, 1907, with applicants chosen by drawing at the Billings land office.
Withdrew more tracts inside the Gila National Forest, north of Fort Bayard, New Mexico, for military purposes to protect the fort's water supply.
Allowed Maude Ward Rockwood to be appointed to a War Department clerical position without examination.
Established the Inyo National Forest on partly timbered public lands in California.
Created the Dragoon National Forest from partly timbered public lands in Arizona Territory.

Reserved all public land within sixty feet of the Mexican border in California, Arizona and New Mexico, keeping it free of obstruction to guard against smuggling; the strip could be used only for public highways.
Redrew California's Diamond Mountain National Forest, adding some partly timbered lands and excluding others.
Enlarged the Plumas National Forest in California with new partly timbered lands plus part of the Diamond Mountain National Forest.
Added partly timbered lands in Arizona Territory to the Santa Rita National Forest.
Allowed Clifford Rose to be appointed private secretary to the Public Printer without examination.
Let the State Department appoint William Phillips of Massachusetts and Percival S. Heintzleman of Pennsylvania as clerks without civil-service examination.
Validated past marriages performed in the Canal Zone by ministers or judicial officers, and authorized them to perform marriages there for couples holding a marriage license.
Announced a commercial agreement with Germany and, from July 1, 1907, lowered duties on listed German products such as argols, brandies, champagne, still wines and paintings.
Cut certain lands out of the Pryor Mountains National Forest in Montana and restored them to the public domain.
Amended the 1896 Consular Regulations on merchandise invoices, so shippers would appear in person before a consul or show original bills only in exceptional cases.

Rewrote Civil Service Rule I to bar federal employees from using official influence in elections and to bar competitive classified workers from active roles in political management or campaigns, while keeping their right to vote and speak privately.
Tightened the civil-service transfer rule, requiring six months' service before any transfer and three years in the old department or independent office for transfers among Washington offices.
Allowed Terence V. Powderly of Washington, D.C., to be appointed chief of the Division of Information in the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization without examination.
Redrew the Magdalena National Forest in New Mexico Territory, adding partly timbered lands and returning others to the public domain.
Removed lands claimed by the Manila Navigation Company from the Mariveles Military Reservation at the entrance to Manila Bay in Bataan, Luzon.
Cut the price of unsold land in the former Devil's Lake Indian Reservation in North Dakota from $4.50 to at least $2.50 an acre, since the remaining tracts were small, hilly or stony.
Excepted from civil-service examination Post Office clerks in charge of contract stations and of stations paying no more than $500 a year.
Let Samuel H. Cunningham, a temporary clerk in the Bureau of Animal Industry, be appointed permanently regardless of his standing on the eligible register.
Allowed George S. Fox, a bookkeeper in the Isthmian service, to be transferred to a classified clerical position in the United States.
Named George W. Woodruff acting Secretary of the Interior.
Created a Committee on Grades and Salaries, with one employee from each department and independent office, to prepare consistent salary estimates for Congress.
Ordered Mattie R. Tyler appointed a clerk at $800 a year in the Norfolk, Virginia, post office, waiving the usual civil-service eligibility rules.
Allowed Forest Service and Biological Survey employees to take state and territorial posts enforcing forest, stock and game laws, and let state foresters serve as Forest Service collaborators.
Set out the rules for passports: only the Secretary of State issues them, at a one-dollar fee, on a sworn written application stating the applicant's birth, residence and travel plans.
Revised the June 3 amendment to Civil Service Rule I, restating the ban on using official influence in elections and on classified employees taking active part in political campaigns.
Let Mary A. Greenstreet, a temporary War Department clerk, be selected from the clerk register for permanent appointment.
Amended Executive Order 469 on promotions in the consular service.
Broadened a civil-service exception covering quarantine attendants, acting assistant surgeons and sanitary inspectors hired for quarantine duty during epidemics.
Allowed John S. Drukker, a former temporary employee, to be reinstated as a pressman at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without regard to civil-service rules.
Classified most civil service positions of the Army Quartermaster's Department at Honolulu, letting approved current employees stay and become eligible for transfer after three years.
Extended the June 13 order so other Agriculture Department employees could hold state and territorial posts, and state officials could take Department appointments, with the Secretary's approval.
Moved purchasing for the Isthmian Canal Commission under the Army's Chief of Engineers from July 1, 1907, with a Purchasing Department in the Commission's Washington offices.
Allowed Horace W. Mitchell to move from a Marine Corps pay clerkship in the Philippines to a classified clerk position in Berkeley, California, without regard to civil-service rules.
Enlarged the Trabuco Canyon National Forest in California with partly timbered lands and changed its name from Trabuco Canon.
Added partly timbered lands in Arizona Territory to the Black Mesa National Forest.
Enlarged the Malate Barracks Military Reservation in Manila.
Let Aksel Hansen be employed by the Census Bureau on experimental work developing tabulating machinery, without a civil-service examination.
Expanded the Santa Catalina National Forest in Arizona Territory to include more partly timbered land.
Removed certain lands from the Alexander Archipelago National Forest in Alaska and returned them to the public domain, protecting existing valid rights.

Created the Chugach National Forest in Alaska, covering public land from Cape Puget along the Chugach Mountains to the Copper River and Cape Cleare, with islands, excepting circles around towns such as Valdez and Orca.
Allowed Margaret F. Sterne to be appointed a Treasury Department clerk without meeting civil-service rules.
Allowed Alice V. Fought to be appointed a Treasury Department clerk without meeting civil-service rules.
Issued rules for the Dominican customs receivership under the 1907 convention, placing it under the Bureau of Insular Affairs and having the President appoint and pay the General Receiver and staff.
Allowed William S. Harris to be reinstated as an examiner in the New York appraiser of merchandise's office, despite more than a year's separation.
Let Harry T. Paterson, a former Reclamation Service employee, be appointed junior civil engineer in the Engineer Department at large without the usual reinstatement and transfer limits.
Corrected the boundaries of the Signal Corps reservation at Old Woman, Alaska, which had been described in error in a 1905 order.
Revoked the June 11, 1907, order that had allowed George S. Fox to transfer from the Isthmian Canal service to the federal classified service.
Gave the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission until March 2, 1908, to finish its work.
Set aside the mud-lump islets at the mouths of the Mississippi River in Louisiana as Tern Islands Reservation, a preserve and breeding ground for native birds.
Allowed Frank Huntington to be appointed to an Agriculture Department position, using his long experience editing technical and scientific articles, without regard to civil-service rules.
Excused federal per diem employees and day laborers from work on Labor Day, making it a holiday for them for all purposes.
Opened ceded Lower Brule Indian Reservation lands in South Dakota to homestead settlement at appraised value, with applicants filing affidavits in the Pierre land district for a drawing.
Moved part of the Lower Brule Indian Reservation in South Dakota from the Chamberlain land district to the Pierre land district.
Authorized the classification of A. J. Robinson as train-master in the Army Quartermaster's Department at large.
Allowed the Bureau of Standards chemist post left open by Dr. William A. Noyes's resignation to be filled without civil-service examination.
Set the salaries of Isthmian Canal Commissioners Lt. Col. W. C. Gorgas and Jackson Smith at $14,000 a year, effective August 12, 1907.
Let W. Dawson Johnston, a Library of Congress employee, transfer to the Bureau of Education as collector and compiler of statistics and librarian, without regard to civil-service rules.
Reorganized the Isthmian Canal Commission's accounts, abolishing the General and Local Auditor posts and creating an Examiner of Accounts on the Isthmus and an Assistant Examiner in Washington.
Set up the Isthmian Canal Commission's Washington office, listing which officers work there and putting the General Purchasing Officer in charge of the offices.
